Nirmala: hey, any update on the vendor report? you said friday 🙂
Tenzin: yes sorry! the data came in late from finance
Tenzin: also the template changed so i had to redo the charts
Nirmala: oh ok. finance said they sent it wednesday though?
Tenzin: right, but it was the wrong format
Tenzin: and honestly the deadline was always unrealistic, nobody could do it by friday
Tenzin: plus i was covering for Arun on tuesday
Nirmala: that's a lot. is something else going on? no judgement
Tenzin: ...
Tenzin: i got stuck on the analysis and didn't want to say 😔
Nirmala: ah. want to go through it together at 3?
Tenzin: yes please

qa.q: When did finance say they sent the data?
qa.a: Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have been thinking as Tenzin's reasons kept piling up?
qa.a: Nirmala seemed to sense that the shifting reasons hid something uncomfortable, so Nirmala asked gently instead of arguing each one.

qa.q: Which choice of Nirmala's got to the real problem?
qa.a: Asking "is something else going on? no judgement" instead of checking each excuse, which made it safe for Tenzin to admit being stuck.

qa.q: Why might Tenzin have found it hard to say 'i got stuck'?
qa.a: Admitting being stuck may have felt embarrassing, so a string of outside reasons felt safer than owning the struggle.

grounding: In a chat, a colleague notices a peer's reasons for a late report keep shifting and gently asks what is really going on.

At the cooperative seed store in Dharwad district, Shankar had promised the farmers' group their order by Monday. His colleague Lokesh had said he'd arrange the tempo.
On Tuesday morning Shankar asked where the tempo was. Lokesh leaned on the counter. "The driver's mother was sick." A minute later: "Actually, the road near Hebballi is broken, so it wasn't safe." Then: "And anyway, the farmers won't sow till the rains come, so Monday didn't really matter."
Each reason was neat, and each was different. Shankar noticed Lokesh kept straightening a receipt book that didn't need straightening.
"Lokesh," Shankar said, "did you forget to call?"
Lokesh's shoulders dropped. "I forgot."

qa.q: What had Lokesh said he would arrange?
qa.a: The tempo.

qa.q: What does Lokesh straightening the receipt book suggest?
qa.a: It hints that Lokesh felt uneasy beneath the neat reasons, perhaps embarrassed that he had simply forgotten to call.

qa.q: What did Shankar choose to do once he noticed the reasons changing?
qa.a: Rather than arguing each excuse, Shankar asked one simple, direct question, which gave Lokesh room to admit the real cause 👍

qa.q: How might the farmers' group see Monday's missed delivery?
qa.a: They may feel let down and wonder whether the store keeps its word, whatever reasons are given.

grounding: At a small-town seed store a worker notices his colleague's reasons for a missed delivery keep changing, and asks the simple question underneath.

passage:
In their Toronto office, Rania stopped by Jin's desk on Friday. "Did you get to my slides? You said Thursday."
Jin launched in. First, the client call ran long. Then the remote connection kept dropping. Then, actually, it made more sense to wait for the new colours, which weren't final. By the fourth reason he was talking faster, and none of them matched the one before.
Rania noticed he hadn't looked up from his screen once. The logic was tidy. Too tidy.
"Jin," she said, "no stress. Is it just a heavy week?"
He breathed out. "I said yes to too many things. I'm drowning a bit."
"Okay. Can you do Monday?"
"Monday. Yes. Thank you."

qa.q: When had Jin said he would look at the slides?
qa.a: Thursday.

qa.q: What did Rania think the too-tidy reasons suggested?
qa.a: Rania read the too-tidy, changing reasons as a sign that Jin was uncomfortable about something he hadn't said.

qa.q: Which choice of Rania's helped Jin say what was really wrong?
qa.a: She stayed calm and asked a gentle, open question about his week instead of pointing out that the excuses didn't match.

qa.q: What might the week have felt like for Jin?
qa.a: Jin was overloaded after saying yes to too much, and probably embarrassed to admit he was drowning, so excuses felt safer at first.

grounding: In an office abroad a colleague hears a peer's shifting, tidy reasons for a missed review and gently asks what is really going on.

passage:
At the physiotherapy clinic on Monday, Indu asked Vaibhav about the new appointment rota he had promised by Friday.
"Right, so," he began. "The printer jammed on Thursday, so I couldn't check the old sheets. Then the booking software updated. And honestly it made more sense to wait for the leave list, because Dr Mehra's dates keep changing."
On Wednesday she asked again. This time it was the software, then a patient who needed extra time, then a new idea about moving everyone to half-hour slots.
Each explanation was neat and sensible. But Indu noticed they never repeated, and that Vaibhav talked faster the longer he went on, eyes on his screen. Something about this rota seemed to make him uneasy.
She pulled up a chair. "Is there a part of the rota that's hard to sort? We could look at it together."

qa.q: What reasons did Vaibhav give on Monday for the late rota?
qa.a: The printer jammed on Thursday, the booking software updated, and it made more sense to wait for the leave list.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's faster talking suggest about how he might feel?
qa.a: It suggests he may feel uneasy or embarrassed about the rota, and the neat reasons help him avoid facing whatever part is hard.

qa.q: Which choice by Indu gave the best chance of getting the rota done?
qa.a: Instead of arguing with each reason, Indu pulled up a chair and offered to look at the hard part together, which makes it safer for Vaibhav to admit what is stuck.

qa.q: If you were Vaibhav, what might you want when Indu pulls up a chair?
qa.a: Probably relief that nobody is picking apart the shifting excuses, and a chance to say which part of the rota is actually the problem.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a peer's neat but ever-changing reasons for a slipped promise and reading them as a sign of discomfort underneath.

passage:
Subject: Thursday, and the launch plan

Hi Keerthana,

I've been thinking about our team meeting on Thursday. When Nikhil asked about the launch plan you'd promised for the first, you explained so carefully: the vendor was slow, then there was the budget freeze, and then it made sense to wait for the new timeline. Each reason sounded fine. Only afterwards did I notice they were different from the ones you gave me on Monday.

I'm not writing to catch you out. I've done the same myself, built a very tidy explanation around something I felt awkward about. So I wondered if the plan is stuck on something that's hard to say in a meeting.

If it is, I'd be glad to sit with you over lunch and look at it. No need to explain anything first.

Ayesha

qa.q: Which reasons did Keerthana give in Thursday's meeting?
qa.a: The vendor was slow, then there was the budget freeze, and then it made sense to wait for the new timeline.

qa.q: What does Ayesha suspect is going on for Keerthana, and why?
qa.a: Ayesha suspects Keerthana feels awkward or stuck about the plan, because the careful reasons changed between Monday and Thursday.

qa.q: Why is Ayesha's choice to write privately, rather than challenge the reasons in the meeting, a good one?
qa.a: A private, non-accusing note lets Keerthana save face and admit what is stuck, and the lunch offer gives a practical way forward.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel reading "I'm not writing to catch you out"?
qa.a: Keerthana might feel exposed at first that the shifting reasons were noticed, but also relieved to be offered help instead of blame.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague who hears a peer's polished, shifting reasons for a missed promise and treats the tidy logic as a hint of discomfort rather than proof of lying.
